Alright, let me think through this.

My family has maybe 12 mu of flat land here on the plain. We've been growing wheat and corn together for as long as I can remember — my father did it, his father did it. That rotation makes sense here. Wheat in winter, corn in summer, same fields. Two harvests a year. I can sell grain to the purchasing station in town.

I don't know much about fancy new things. But I know wheat needs water in spring — I'll run the pump four times like I usually do: before winter sets in, then at greening, jointing, and heading. Corn is easier, it rains more in summer, so maybe twice.

For fertilizer — I'll use the compound fertilizer bags from the co-op at planting, then add urea on top when the crop is growing. I've heard I maybe use a bit much but the dealer says more is safer and I don't want a bad harvest. The whole family depends on this.

For wheat I'll use the improved variety seeds from the county seed station — Jimai or whatever they're pushing this year. For corn I'll buy hybrid seed bags, the郑单 type I've been using for years. Good yield, familiar.

I'll use the rotary tiller before planting wheat to break up the stalks. For corn after wheat, I'll plant directly — saves diesel and time.

decision.reasoning_summary: I farm 12 mu of flat land in Quzhou using the standard winter wheat and summer corn double-crop rotation that every family here does. I plant improved wheat varieties from the county seed station in October after rotary tilling the corn residue, irrigating four times through the season, and applying compound fertilizer plus urea top-dressing. After wheat harvest in June I plant hybrid corn directly into the stubble without tilling to save time and fuel, relying mainly on summer rain with two supplemental irrigations. Fertilizer rates follow what the input dealer recommends and what I have seen work on my land, erring on the side of enough rather than too little, since a poor harvest would be very hard on the family.
